Small Solitons and Multi-Solitons in Generalized Davey-Stewartson System

Mengxue Bai ††thanks: E-mail: mengxuebai@163.com Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Sichuan, Chengdu 611731, China    Jian Zhang ††thanks: Corresponding author. E-mail: zhangjian@uestc.edu.cn Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Sichuan, Chengdu 611731, China    Shihui Zhu ††thanks: E-mail: shihuizhumath@163.com Affiliation: School of Mathematical Sciences, Sichuan Normal University, Sichuan, Chengdu 610066, China

Abstract: This paper is concerned with the generalized Davey-Stewarston system in two dimensional space. Existence and stability of small solitons are proved by solving two correlative constrained variational problems and spectrum analysis. In addition, multi-solitons with different speeds are constructed by bootstrap argument.

Mathematics Subject Classification (2010): 35Q35, 76W05, 35B65

Keywords: Davey-Stewartson system, variational method, spectrum analysis, small soliton, soliton resolution

1 Introduction

Consider the generalized Davey-Stewartson system in two dimensional space,

i​φt+Δ​φ+|φ|p−1​φ+E1​(|φ|2)​φ=0,(t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ2.\displaystyle i\varphi_{t}+\Delta\varphi+\lvert\varphi\rvert^{p-1}\varphi+E_{1}(\lvert\varphi\rvert^{2})\varphi=0,\;\;(t,\;x)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}. (1.1)

Here 1<p<∞1<p<\infty and E1E_{1} is the singular integral operator with symbol σ1​(ξ)=ξ12|ξ|2\sigma_{1}(\xi)=\frac{\xi^{2}_{1}}{\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}}, ξ∈ℝ2\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, that is E1​(φ)​(x)=ℱ−1​(ξ12|ξ|2​ℱ​(φ)​(ξ))E_{1}(\varphi)(x)=\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\frac{\xi^{2}_{1}}{\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}}\mathcal{F}(\varphi)(\xi)), where ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ−1\mathcal{F}^{-1} represent the Fourier transform and Fourier inverse transform on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} respectively, and ℱ⁡(φ)​(ξ)=12​π​∫e−i​x​ξ​φ​(x)​𝑑x\mathcal{F}(\varphi)(\xi)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int e^{-ix\xi}\varphi(x)dx. Here and hereafter we denote ∫ℝ2⋅dx\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\cdot dx by ∫⋅dx\int\cdot dx, L2​(ℝ2)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) by L2L^{2} and H1​(ℝ2)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{2}) by H1H^{1}.

(1.1) origins from fluid mechanics, and it models the evolution of weakly nonlinear water waves having a predominant direction of travel. More precisely, (1.1) is the extension of the Davey-Stewartson systems in the elliptic-elliptic case, namely

{i​φt+λ​φx1​x1+μ​φx2​x2=a​|φ|2​φ+b1​φ​ϕx1,ν​ϕx1​x1+ϕx2​x2=−b2​(|φ|2)x1\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}&i\varphi_{t}+\lambda\varphi_{x_{1}x_{1}}+\mu\varphi_{x_{2}x_{2}}=a\lvert\varphi\rvert^{2}\varphi+b_{1}\varphi\phi_{x_{1}},\\ &\nu\phi_{x_{1}x_{1}}+\phi_{x_{2}x_{2}}=-b_{2}(\lvert\varphi\rvert^{2})_{x_{1}}\end{array}\right. (1.2)

(a∈ℝ,λ,μ,ν,b1​a​n​d​b2>0a\in\mathbb{R},\;\lambda,\;\mu,\;\nu,\;b_{1}\;and\;b_{2}>0) which describes the time evolution of two-dimensional surface of water wave having a propagation preponderantly in the x1x_{1}-direction (see [7, 13, 16, 25]).

Ghidaglia and Saut[13] showed the local well-posedness of the Cauchy problem of (1.1) in the natural energy space H1H^{1} for p=3p=3, then Guo and Wang [16] generalized this result to 1<p<∞1<p<\infty. Ozawa [24] constructed the exact blow up solutions of the Cauchy problem of (1.1) for p=3p=3 (also see the numerical simulation result of Sulem C. and Sulem P. L.[31]). By Ghidaglia and Saut[13] as well as Ohta [27], it was known that the Cauchy problem of (1.1) has blow up solutions to appear for 1<p<∞1<p<\infty. In addition, Gan and Zhang [12] studied sharp threshold of blow up and global existence for the Cauchy problem of (1.1). In terms of Zhang’s argument[38], Zhu [39] got global existence of small solutions with the mass for the Cauchy problem of (1.1).

For ω>0\omega>0, consider the following nonlinear elliptic equation

Δ​u+|u|p−1​u+E1​(|u|2)​u=ω​u,u∈H1\displaystyle\Delta u+\lvert u\rvert^{p-1}u+E_{1}(\lvert u\rvert^{2})u=\omega u,\;\;u\in H^{1} (1.3)

If u⁡(x)u(x) is a non-trivial solution of (1.3), then ei​ω​t​u​(x)e^{i\omega t}u(x) is a soliton of (1.1).

Cipolatti [7] proved the existence of positive solutions of (1.3) by means of P. L. Lion’s concentration-compactness method (see [20, 21]). Then Cipolatti (see [8]), Ohta [27], Gan and Zhang [12] showed the instability of the solitons of (1.1) for 3≤p<∞3\leq p<\infty respectively by different methods. Because of the singular operator E1E_{1} in (1.3) (see [31]), the uniqueness of positive solutions for (1.3) is still open. Under the assumption of uniqueness of positive solutions of (1.3), Ohta [25] proved that for 1<p<31<p<3, there exists a sequence of frequency ωn>0\omega_{n}>0 such that ωn→0\omega_{n}\rightarrow 0 and the solitons ei​ωn​t​Qne^{i\omega_{n}t}Q_{n} are stable, where QnQ_{n} is the unique positive solution of (1.3) corresponding to ωn>0\omega_{n}>0. Moreover Ohta [27] got the stability of the solitons generated by the set of minimizers of the associated variational problem. From [8, 26, 12], the instability of solitons for (1.1) has gotten a comprehensive study. And from [25, 27], further study to stability of solitons for (1.1) becomes an interesting topic. In this paper we develop some new technologyies to study stability of solitons for (1.1).

For u∈H1\{0}u\in H^{1}\backslash\{0\}, we define the funtional

J⁡(u)=(∫|u|2​𝑑x)​(∫|∇u|2​𝑑x)∫E1​(|u|2)​|u|2​𝑑x.\displaystyle J(u)=\frac{(\int\lvert u\rvert^{2}dx)(\int\lvert\nabla u\rvert^{2}dx)}{\int E_{1}(\lvert u\rvert^{2})\lvert u\rvert^{2}dx}. (1.4)

Then we consider the variational problem

dJ=inf{u∈H1\{0}}J(u).\displaystyle d_{J}=inf_{\{u\in H^{1}\backslash\{0\}\}}J(u). (1.5)

It is known that (1.5) possesses a positive minimizer u∈H1u\in H^{1} (see [39]). Therefore dJd_{J} is a positive constant. Moreover, for arbitrary u∈H1u\in H^{1}, one has the sharp interpolation inequality:

∫E1(|u|2)|u|2dx≤1dJ∫|∇u|2dx∫|u|2dx.\displaystyle\int E_{1}(\lvert u\rvert^{2})\lvert u\rvert^{2}dx\leq\frac{1}{d_{J}}\int\rvert\nabla u\lvert^{2}dx\int\rvert u\lvert^{2}dx. (1.6)

Let

ωJ=sup{ω∈ℝ|∥Qω∥L2<2​dJ},\displaystyle\omega_{J}=sup\{\omega\in\mathbb{R}\big\lvert\;\|Q_{\omega}\|_{L^{2}}<\sqrt{2d_{J}}\}, (1.7)

where QωQ_{\omega} is the positive solution of (1.3). Firstly we can prove that ωJ>0\omega_{J}>0. Then we prove the following crucial results of stability of solitons for (1.1).

Theorem A. Let ω∈(0,wJ)\omega\in(0,w_{J}), 1<p<31<p<3 and Qω​(x)Q_{\omega}(x) is the positive solution of (1.3). Suppose that the positive solution of (1.3) is unique, then the small solitons ei​ω​t​Qω​(x)e^{i\omega t}Q_{\omega}(x) of (1.1) is orbitally stable. Moreover it is true that dd​ω​∫Qω2​𝑑x>0\frac{d}{d\omega}\int Q^{2}_{\omega}dx>0 for all ω∈(0,ωJ)\omega\in(0,\omega_{J}).

In order to prove Theorem A, we construct and solve two correlative constrained variational problems. Then we ascertain frequency from mass by establishing a one-to-one mapping. Finally we bridge Grillakis-Shatah-Strauss method [15] and Cazenave-Lions method [4] for stability of the solitons by spectrum analysis. It is clear that Theorem A includes the results in [25, 27]. Moreover technologies developed in this paper can be used to determine frequency from the prescribed mass in the normalized solution problems (see [1, 2, 3, 38]). We discuss this problem in other papers.

In terms of Co^\widehat{o}te and Le Coz’s arguments [9], Wang and Cui [35] constructed the high speed excited multi-solitons of (1.1). Multi-solitons are concerned with the famous soliton resolution conjecture, which is emphasized in Tao [32], Zakharov and Shabat [37]. The stability of solitons and the soliton resolution problems are crucial topics in understanding the dynamics of nonlinear dispersive evolution equations (see Tao [33]). Therefore we use the stable solitons of (1.1) obtained in Theorem A to construct multi-solitons with different speeds for (1.1)(1.1) according to Martel, Merle and Tsai’s scheme (see [22, 23]). We prove the following theorem.

Theorem B: Let 1<p<31<p<3. For K≥2K\geq 2 and k=1, 2,⋯,Kk=1,\;2,\;\cdot\cdot\cdot,\;K, taking ωk∈(0,ωJ)\omega_{k}\in(0,\;\omega_{J}), γk∈ℝ\gamma_{k}\in\mathbb{R}, xk∈ℝ2x_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, vk∈ℝ2v_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} with vk≠vk′v_{k}\neq v_{k^{\prime}} to k≠k′k\neq k^{\prime} and

Rk​(t,x)=Qωk​(x−xk−vk​t)​ei⁡(12​vk​x−14​|vk|2​t+ωk​t+γk)\displaystyle R_{k}(t,x)=Q_{\omega_{k}}(x-x_{k}-v_{k}t)e^{i(\frac{1}{2}v_{k}x-\frac{1}{4}\lvert v_{k}\rvert^{2}t+\omega_{k}t+\gamma_{k})} (1.8)

with (t,x)∈ℝ×ℝ2(t,x)\in\ \mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{2}, there exists a solution φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,\;x) of (1.1) such that

limt→+∞‖φ⁡(t)−∑k=1KRk​(t)‖H1=0.\displaystyle\lim\limits_{t\rightarrow+\infty}\|\varphi(t)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}R_{k}(t)\|_{H^{1}}=0. (1.9)

The solution φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,\;x) of (1.1) holding (1.9) is called multi-soliton of (1.1).

The rest contents of this paper are organized as follows. In section 2, we show global existence of small solutions of the Cauchy problem for (1.1) and existence of solitons for (1.1). In section 3, by solving two correlative constrained variational problems, we establish a one-to-one mapping between mass and frequency. In section 4, we prove orbital stability of small solitons depending on mass for (1.1). Moreover by spectrum analysis, we communicate the relationship between Cazenave-Lions method [4] and Grillakis-Shatah-Strauss method [15]. In addition, we get orbital stability of solitons depending on frequencies ω∈(0,ωJ)\omega\in(0,\omega_{J}) for (1.1). In section 5, we construct multi-solitons with different speeds for (1.1) by all stable solitons in terms of the bootstrap scheme and the uniform backward estimate according to [9, 22, 23, 35].

2 Well-Posedness

For t0∈ℝt_{0}\in\mathbb{R}, we impose the initial data of (1.1) as follows.

φ⁡(t0,x)=φ0​(x),x∈ℝ2.\displaystyle\varphi(t_{0},x)=\varphi_{0}(x),\;\;\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}. (2.1)

In H1H^{1}, we define the energy functional

E⁡(φ)=∫|∇φ|2​𝑑x−2p+1​∫|φ|p+1​𝑑x−12​∫E1​(|φ|2)​|φ|2​𝑑x;\displaystyle E(\varphi)=\int\lvert\nabla\varphi\rvert^{2}dx-\frac{2}{p+1}\int\lvert\varphi\rvert^{p+1}dx-\frac{1}{2}\int E_{1}(\lvert\varphi\rvert^{2})\lvert\varphi\rvert^{2}dx; (2.2)

the mass functional

M⁡(φ)=∫|φ|2​𝑑x;\displaystyle M(\varphi)=\int\lvert\varphi\rvert^{2}dx; (2.3)

and the momentum functional

P(φ)=Im∫φ¯∇φdx.\displaystyle P(\varphi)=Im\int\overline{\varphi}\nabla\varphi dx. (2.4)

First we have the following lemma by Zhu [39].

Lemma 2.1. Define the variational problem

dJ=inf{ϕ∈H1\{0}}J(ϕ)withJ(ϕ)=(∫|ϕ|2​𝑑x)​(∫|∇ϕ|2​𝑑x)∫E1​(|ϕ|2)​|ϕ|2​𝑑x.\displaystyle d_{J}=inf_{\{\phi\in H^{1}\backslash\{0\}\}}J(\phi)\;\;\;with\;J(\phi)=\frac{(\int\lvert\phi\rvert^{2}dx)(\int\lvert\nabla\phi\rvert^{2}dx)}{\int E_{1}(\lvert\phi\rvert^{2})\lvert\phi\rvert^{2}dx}. (2.5)

Then (2.5) possesses a nontrivial minimizer and dJ>0d_{J}>0. Moreover for ϕ∈H1\phi\in H^{1}, we have the sharp Gagliardo-Nirenberg type inequality

∫E1(|ϕ|2)|ϕ|2dx≤1dJ∫|∇ϕ|2dx∫|ϕ|2dx.\displaystyle\int E_{1}(\lvert\phi\rvert^{2})\lvert\phi\rvert^{2}dx\leq\frac{1}{d_{J}}\int\rvert\nabla\phi\lvert^{2}dx\int\rvert\phi\lvert^{2}dx. (2.6)

Then we have the following global well-posedness for (1.1) with small mass.

Theorem 2.2. Let 1<p<31<p<3, φ0∈H1\varphi_{0}\in H^{1} and ‖φ0‖L2<2​dJ\|\varphi_{0}\|_{L^{2}}<\sqrt{2d_{J}}. Then the Cauchy problem (1.1)-(2.1) possesses a unique global solution φ⁡(t,x)∈C⁡(ℝ,H1)\varphi(t,x)\in C(\mathbb{R},\;H^{1}) with mass conservation M⁡(φ)=M⁡(φ0)M(\varphi)=M(\varphi_{0}), energy conservation E⁡(φ)=E⁡(φ0)E(\varphi)=E(\varphi_{0}) and momentum conservation P⁡(φ)=P⁡(φ0)P(\varphi)=P(\varphi_{0}) for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}.
Proof. By [6] and [14], for φ0∈H1\varphi_{0}\in H^{1} with ‖φ0‖L2<2​dJ\|\varphi_{0}\|_{L^{2}}<\sqrt{2d_{J}}, there exists a unique solution φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,\;x) of the Cauchy problem (1.1)-(2.1) in C⁡((−T,T),H1)C((-T,\;T);H^{1}) to some T>0T>0 (maximal existence time). And φ⁡(t,⋅)\varphi(t,\;\cdot) satisfies mass conservation M⁡(φ)=M⁡(φ0)M(\varphi)=M(\varphi_{0}), energy conservation E⁡(φ)=E⁡(φ0)E(\varphi)=E(\varphi_{0}) and momentum conservation P⁡(φ)=P⁡(φ0)P(\varphi)=P(\varphi_{0}) for all t∈(−T,T)t\in(-T,\;T). Furthermore one has the alternatives: T=∞T=\infty (global existence) or else T<∞T<\infty and l​i​mt→T​‖φ‖H1=∞lim_{t\rightarrow T}\|\varphi\|_{H^{1}}=\infty (blow up). Thus from (2.2), (2.6), we have that

E⁡(φ)≥(1−12​dJ​∫|φ|2​𝑑x)​∫|∇φ|2​𝑑x−2p+1​∫|φ|p+1​𝑑x.\displaystyle E(\varphi)\geq(1-\frac{1}{2d_{J}}\int\lvert\varphi\rvert^{2}dx)\int\lvert\nabla\varphi\rvert^{2}dx-\frac{2}{p+1}\int\lvert\varphi\rvert^{p+1}dx. (2.7)

From the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality

∫|φ|p+1​𝑑x≤C⁡(p)​(∫|φ|2​𝑑x)​(∫|∇φ|2​𝑑x)p−12,φ∈H1,\displaystyle\int\lvert\varphi\rvert^{p+1}dx\leq C(p)(\int\lvert\varphi\rvert^{2}dx)(\int\lvert\nabla\varphi\rvert^{2}dx)^{\frac{p-1}{2}},\;\;\varphi\in H^{1}, (2.8)

mass conservation and energy conservation, (2.7) yields that

C1​∫|∇φ|2​𝑑x−C2​(∫|∇φ|2​𝑑x)p−12≤E⁡(φ0),\displaystyle C_{1}\int\lvert\nabla\varphi\rvert^{2}dx-C_{2}(\int\lvert\nabla\varphi\rvert^{2}dx)^{\frac{p-1}{2}}\leq E(\varphi_{0}), (2.9)

where C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are positive constants only concerning dd and φ0∈H1\varphi_{0}\in H^{1}. From 1<p<31<p<3, ∫|∇φ|2​𝑑x\int\lvert\nabla\varphi\rvert^{2}dx is bounded for t∈(−T,T)t\in(-T,\;T) with any T<∞T<\infty. Therefore combining with the mass conservation, we get that φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,\;x) globally exists in t∈(−∞,∞)t\in(-\infty,\;\infty). Moreover, the mass conservation and the energy conservation, as well as the momentum conservation are true to all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}.

This proves Theorem 2.2.

Theorem 2.3. Let 1<p<31<p<3 and ω∈ℝ\omega\in\mathbb{R}. Then the necessary condition for the nonlinear elliptic equation

Δ​u−ω​u+|u|p−1​u+E1​(|u|2)​u=0,u∈H1\displaystyle\Delta u-\omega u+\lvert u\rvert^{p-1}u+E_{1}(\lvert u\rvert^{2})u=0,\;\;u\in H^{1} (2.10)

to possess nontrivial solutions is ω>0\omega>0.

Proof. Let u⁡(x)u(x) be a nontrivial solution of (2.10). By the Pohozaev’s identity (see [28]), we have that,

−2p+1∫|u|p+1dx−12∫E1(|u|2)|u|2dx+ω∫|u|2dx=0.\displaystyle-\frac{2}{p+1}\int\rvert u\lvert^{p+1}dx-\frac{1}{2}\int E_{1}(\rvert u\lvert^{2})\rvert u\lvert^{2}dx+\omega\int\rvert u\lvert^{2}dx=0. (2.11)

Since

∫E1(|u|2)|u|2dx=∫|u|2ℱ−1(σ1(ξ)ℱ(|u|2))dx=∫σ1(ξ)|ℱ(|u|2)|2dξ>0,\displaystyle\int E_{1}(\rvert u\lvert^{2})\rvert u\lvert^{2}dx=\int\rvert u\lvert^{2}\mathcal{F}^{-1}(\sigma_{1}(\xi)\mathcal{F}(\rvert u\lvert^{2}))dx=\int\sigma_{1}(\xi)\rvert\mathcal{F}(\rvert u\lvert^{2})\lvert^{2}d\xi>0, (2.12)

from (2.11) it follows that ω>0\omega>0.

This proves Theorem 2.3.

From Cipolatti [7] we state the following lemma.

Lemma 2.4. Let 1<p<31<p<3 and ω>0\omega>0. Then the nonlinear elliptic equation (2.10) possesses a positive solution Qω​(x)Q_{\omega}(x), and Qω​(x)Q_{\omega}(x) has exponential decay property with C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0:

|∇Qω​(x)|+|Qω​(x)|≤C1​e−C2​|x|,x∈ℝ2.\displaystyle\lvert\nabla Q_{\omega}(x)\rvert+\lvert Q_{\omega}(x)\rvert\leq C_{1}e^{-C_{2}\lvert x\rvert},\;\;\;x\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{2}. (2.13)

In addition, let Ej,j=1, 2E_{j},\;j=1,\;2 be the pseudo-differential operator with symbol σj​(ξ)=ξ1​ξj|ξ|2\sigma_{j}(\xi)=\frac{\xi_{1}\xi_{j}}{\lvert\xi\rvert^{2}}. Then Ej​(|Qω​(x)|2)E_{j}(\lvert Q_{\omega}(x)\rvert^{2}) has exponential decay property:

|Ej​(|Qω​(x)|2)|≤C1​e−C2​|x|,x∈ℝ2.\displaystyle\lvert E_{j}(\lvert Q_{\omega}(x)\rvert^{2})\rvert\leq C_{1}e^{-C_{2}\lvert x\rvert},\;\;\;x\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{2}. (2.14)

Proof. The proof of (2.13) is from [7]. For reader’s convenience, we give the proof of (2.14) (also see [35]). Let f=ℬ∗|Qω​(x)|2f=\mathcal{B}\ast\lvert Q_{\omega}(x)\rvert^{2}, where ℬ\mathcal{B} is the fundamental solution of the Laplacian. Then ff is a solution of the following equation:

−Δ​f=|Qω​(x)|2.\displaystyle-\Delta f=\lvert Q_{\omega}(x)\rvert^{2}. (2.15)

It is easy to see that

Ej(|Qω(x)|2)=−∂1∂jf,j=1, 2.\displaystyle E_{j}(\lvert Q_{\omega}(x)\rvert^{2})=-\partial_{1}\partial_{j}f,\;\;j=1,\;2. (2.16)

Hence, in order to prove (2.14), it is sufficient to prove the spatial exponential decay of ∂1∂jf\partial_{1}\partial_{j}f. Note that

−Δ∂1∂jf=2Re(∂1∂jQωQ¯ω+∂1Qω∂jQ¯ω),j=1, 2.\displaystyle-\Delta\partial_{1}\partial_{j}f=2Re(\partial_{1}\partial_{j}Q_{\omega}\overline{Q}_{\omega}+\partial_{1}Q_{\omega}\partial_{j}\overline{Q}_{\omega}),\;\;j=1,\;2.

By (2.13), we see that there exists positive constants C1C_{1} such that the absolute value of the right-hand side of the above equation is bounded by C1​e−C2​|x|C_{1}e^{-C_{2}\lvert x\rvert}, let g=g⁡(|x|)g=g(\lvert x\rvert) be the unique radial solution of the problem

−Δ​g=C1​e−ω​|x|,lim|x|→∞g⁡(|x|)=0.\displaystyle-\Delta g=C_{1}e^{-\sqrt{\omega}\lvert x\rvert},\;\;\;\;\lim_{\lvert x\rvert\rightarrow\infty}g(\lvert x\rvert)=0.

A simple computation shows that there exists a polynomial P⁡(x)P(x) such that

|g⁡(|x|)|≤C1​P​(x)​e−C2​|x|,f​o​r​|x|≥0.\displaystyle\lvert g(\lvert x\rvert)\rvert\leq C_{1}P(x)e^{-C_{2}\lvert x\rvert},\;\;for\;\lvert x\rvert\geq 0.

Hence, by using the standard super and sub-solutions method, we obtain |∂1∂jf|≤C1​e−C2​|x|\lvert\partial_{1}\partial_{j}f\rvert\leq C_{1}e^{-C_{2}\lvert x\rvert}.

This completes the proof.

3 Correlative Variational Framework

Firstly we state the profile decomposition theory of a bounded sequence in H1H^{1}, which is proposed by Hmidi and Keraani in [34].

Lemma 3.1. Let {un}n=1+∞\{u_{n}\}_{n=1}^{+\infty} be a bounded sequence in H1H^{1}. Then, there exists a subsequence of {un}n=1+∞\{u_{n}\}_{n=1}^{+\infty} (still denoted by {un}n=1+∞\{u_{n}\}_{n=1}^{+\infty} ) and a sequence {Uj}j=1+∞\{U^{j}\}_{j=1}^{+\infty} in H1H^{1} and a family of {xnj}j=1+∞⊂ℝ2\{x_{n}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{+\infty}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} satisfying the following.
(i) For every j≠kj\neq k, |xnj−xnk|→+∞\lvert x_{n}^{j}-x_{n}^{k}\rvert\rightarrow+\infty as n→+∞n\rightarrow+\infty.
(ii) For every l≥1l\geq 1 and every x∈ℝ2x\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, un​(x)u_{n}(x) can be decomposed by

un​(x)=∑j=1lUj​(x−xnj)+unl,\displaystyle u_{n}(x)=\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}U^{j}(x-x_{n}^{j})+u_{n}^{l},

with the remaining term unl:=unl​(x)u_{n}^{l}:=u_{n}^{l}(x) satisfying

liml→+∞lim supn→+∞‖unl‖Lq​(ℝ2)=0,f​o​r​e​v​e​r​y​q∈(2,+∞).\displaystyle\lim_{l\rightarrow+\infty}\limsup_{n\rightarrow+\infty}\;\|u_{n}^{l}\|_{L^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{2})}=0,\;for\;every\;q\in(2,+\infty).

Moreover, as n→+∞n\rightarrow+\infty,

‖un‖L22=∑j=1l‖Uj‖L22+‖unl‖L22+o⁡(1),‖∇un‖L22=∑j=1l‖∇Uj‖L22+‖∇unl‖L22+o⁡(1),\displaystyle\|u_{n}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}\|U^{j}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|u_{n}^{l}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+o(1),\;\|\nabla u_{n}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}\|\nabla U^{j}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+\|\nabla u_{n}^{l}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}+o(1), (3.1)

where limn→+∞o⁡(1)=0\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow+\infty}o(1)=0.

The sequence {xnj}n=1+∞\{x_{n}^{j}\}_{n=1}^{+\infty} is called to satisfy the orthogonality condition if and only if for every k≠jk\neq j, |xnk−xnj|→+∞​a​s​n→∞\lvert x_{n}^{k}-x_{n}^{j}\rvert\rightarrow+\infty\;\;as\;\;n\rightarrow\infty.

Then we show the following lemma.

Lemma 3.2. Let {Uj}j=1l\{U^{j}\}_{j=1}^{l} be a family of bounded sequences in H1H^{1} and {xnj}n=1+∞\{x_{n}^{j}\}_{n=1}^{+\infty} be a orthogonality sequence in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. We claim that for every 1<p<∞1<p<\infty,

∫(∑j=1lUj​(x−xnj))p+1​𝑑x→∑j=1l∫(Uj​(x−xnj))p+1​𝑑xasn→+∞.\displaystyle\int(\sum_{j=1}^{l}U^{j}(x-x_{n}^{j}))^{p+1}dx\rightarrow\sum_{j=1}^{l}\int(U^{j}(x-x_{n}^{j}))^{p+1}dx\ \ \ {\rm as}\ \ \ n\rightarrow+\infty. (3.2)
∫E1​(|∑j=1lUnj|2)​|∑j=1lUnj|2​𝑑x→∑j=1l∫E1​(|Unj|2)​|Unj|2​𝑑xasn→+∞.\displaystyle\int E_{1}(\lvert\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}U_{n}^{j}\rvert^{2})\lvert\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}U_{n}^{j}\rvert^{2}dx\rightarrow\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}\int E_{1}(\lvert U_{n}^{j}\rvert^{2})\lvert U_{n}^{j}\rvert^{2}dx\ \ \ {\rm as}\ \ \ n\rightarrow+\infty. (3.3)

Proof. We give the proof of (3.2). Then (3.3) can be obtained by the same arguments, (also see [39]). Assume that every UjU^{j} is continuous and compactly supported. From the basic inequality: for every p>1p>1

||∑j=1laj|p+1−∑j=1l|aj|p+1|≤C​∑j≠k|aj|​|ak|p,\lvert\lvert\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}a_{j}\rvert^{p+1}-\sum\limits_{j=1}^{l}\lvert a_{j}\rvert^{p+1}\rvert\leq C\sum\limits_{j\neq k}\lvert a_{j}\rvert\lvert a_{k}\rvert^{p},

we have that it is sufficient to prove that the mixed terms in the left hand side of (3.2) vanish. More precisely, for all j≠kj\neq k, we claim that

∫|Uj|​|Uk|​|Um|p−1​𝑑x→0​a​s​n→+∞.\displaystyle\int\lvert U^{j}\rvert\lvert U^{k}\rvert\lvert U^{m}\rvert^{p-1}dx\rightarrow 0\;\;as\;\;n\rightarrow+\infty. (3.4)

To show (3.4), based on some basic computations we deduce the following inequality

∫|Uj​Uk|​|Um|​𝑑x\displaystyle\int\lvert U^{j}U^{k}\rvert\lvert U^{m}\rvert dx ≤C(∫|UjUk|p+12dx)2p+1∫|∇Um|p−1dx\displaystyle\leq C\left(\int\lvert U^{j}U^{k}\rvert^{\frac{p+1}{2}}dx\right)^{\frac{2}{p+1}}\int\rvert\nabla U^{m}\lvert^{p-1}dx
≤C​(∫|Uj​Uk|p+12​𝑑x)2p+1.\displaystyle\leq C\left(\int\lvert U^{j}U^{k}\rvert^{\frac{p+1}{2}}dx\right)^{\frac{2}{p+1}}. (3.5)

From Lemma 3.1, we deduce that

∫|Uj​Uk|p+12​𝑑x=∫|Uj​(y−(xnj−xnk))​Uk​(y)|p+12​𝑑y→0asn→+∞.\displaystyle\int\lvert U^{j}U^{k}\rvert^{\frac{p+1}{2}}dx=\int\lvert U^{j}(y-(x_{n}^{j}-x_{n}^{k}))U^{k}(y)\rvert^{\frac{p+1}{2}}dy\rightarrow 0\ \ {\rm as}\ \ n\rightarrow+\infty. (3.6)

Finally, from (3.5) and (3.6), (3.4) can be obtained.

This completes the proof of Lemma 3.2.

Remark 3.4. In fact, Ohta [26] solved the variational problem (3.7) with small mass by the concentration compactness principle [20, 21]. But here we solve the variational problem (3.7) with definite mass 0<m<2​dJ0<m<2d_{J} by the profile decomposition.

Theorem 3.6. Let 1<p<31<p<3 and Qm∈H1Q_{m}\in H^{1} be a positive minimizer of (3.7). Suppose that the positive solution of (2.10) is unique for every ω>0\omega>0. with

∫Qω′2​𝑑x=∫Qm2​𝑑x=m;\displaystyle\int Q^{2}_{\omega^{\prime}}dx=\int Q^{2}_{m}dx=m; (3.65)

E⁡(Qm)<E⁡(Qω′).\displaystyle E(Q_{m})<E(Q_{\omega^{\prime}}). (3.69)

By (3.65), (3.66) and (3.68), Theorem 3.8 derives that

E⁡(Qω′)+ω′​∫Qω′2​𝑑x≤E⁡(Qm)+ω′​∫Qm2​𝑑x.\displaystyle E(Q_{\omega^{\prime}})+\omega^{\prime}\int Q^{2}_{\omega^{\prime}}dx\leq E(Q_{m})+\omega^{\prime}\int Q^{2}_{m}dx. (3.70)

From (3.65), it is clear that (3.70) is contradictory with (3.69). Therefore it is necessary that ωm=ω′\omega_{m}=\omega^{\prime}. It turns that for ω∈(0,ωJ)\omega\in(0,\omega_{J}) and positive solution Qω​(x)Q_{\omega}(x) of (2.10), we have that

d​md​ω=dd​ω​∫Qω2​𝑑x≠0.\displaystyle\frac{dm}{d\omega}=\frac{d}{d\omega}\int Q^{2}_{\omega}dx\neq 0.

This completes the proof of Theorem 3.9.

Theorem 3.10. Let μ\mu be the set of all Lagrange multipliers corresponding to the all positive minimizers of (3.7).Then μ=(0,ωJ)\mu=(0,\omega_{J}), where ωJ\omega_{J} is defined as (1.7). In addition μJ=(0,ωJ)\mu_{J}=(0,\omega_{J}), where μJ\mu_{J} is defined as (3.31).

Proof. Theorem 3.5 derives that μ⊂μJ⊂(0,ωJ)\mu\subset\mu_{J}\subset(0,\omega_{J}). Now suppose that ω∈(0,ωJ)\omega\in(0,\omega_{J}). By Theorem 3.8, this ω\omega determines a unique m∈(0,2​dJ)m\in(0,2d_{J}), and this mm determines a unique ωm∈μ\omega_{m}\in\mu. Then this ωm\omega_{m} can only be ω\omega, that is ωm=ω\omega_{m}=\omega. Thus (0,ωJ)⊂μ(0,\omega_{J})\subset\mu. Therefore μ=(0,ωJ)\mu=(0,\omega_{J}). It follows that μ=(0,ωJ)=μJ\mu=(0,\omega_{J})=\mu_{J}.

This proves Theorem 3.10.

Remark 3.11. Theorem 3.9 shows that for m<2​dJm<2d_{J}, the normalized solution problem (2.10) with ∫|u|2dx=m\int\rvert u\lvert^{2}dx=m possesses a unique ωm∈(0,ωJ)\omega_{m}\in(0,\omega_{J}) such that QmQ_{m} is the unique positive solution of (2.10) with ω=ωm\omega=\omega_{m}. It gives a positive answer that for (2.10), the mapping from the prescribed mass mm to the Lagrange multiplier, that is the soliton frequency ω\omega is injective. Moreover the approach introduced here can be used to deal with more nonlinear Schrödinger equations.

4 Orbital Stability of Small Solitons

Theorem 4.1. The soliton ei​ω​t​u​(x)e^{i\omega t}u(x) in Theorem 3.6 holds the orbital stability, i.e. for arbitrary ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that for any φ0∈H1\varphi_{0}\in H^{1} and 0<∫|φ0|2​𝑑x<2​dJ0<\int\lvert\varphi_{0}\rvert^{2}dx<2d_{J}, if

inf{θ∈ℝ,y∈ℝ2}∥φ0(⋅)−ei​θu(⋅+y)∥H1<δ,\displaystyle inf_{\{\theta\in\mathbb{R},\;\;y\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\}}\|\varphi_{0}(\cdot)-e^{i\theta}u(\cdot+y)\|_{H^{1}}<\delta, (4.1)

then the solution φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,\;x) of the Cauchy problem (1.1)-(2.1) satisfies

inf{θ∈ℝ,y∈ℝ2}∥φ(t,⋅)−ei​θu(⋅+y)∥H1<ε,t∈ℝ.\displaystyle inf_{\{\theta\in\mathbb{R},\;\;y\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\}}\|\varphi(t,\cdot)-e^{i\theta}u(\cdot+y)\|_{H^{1}}<\varepsilon,\;\;t\in\mathbb{R}. (4.2)

Proof. By Theorem 3.6, it is clear that for arbitrary u∈Smu\in S_{m} one has that

Sm={ei​θu(⋅+y),θ∈ℝ,y∈ℝ2}.\displaystyle S_{m}=\{e^{i\theta}u(\cdot+y),\;\;\theta\in\mathbb{R},\;\;y\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\}. (4.3)

In terms of Theorem 2.1, for any φ0∈H1\varphi_{0}\in H^{1}, the Cauchy problem (1.1)-(2.1) possesses a unique global solution φ⁡(t,x)∈C⁡(ℝ,H1)\varphi(t,\;x)\in C(\mathbb{R,}\;H^{1}) with mass conservation M⁡(φ)=M⁡(φ0)M(\varphi)=M(\varphi_{0}) and energy conservation E⁡(φ)=E⁡(φ0)E(\varphi)=E(\varphi_{0}) for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}.

Now arguing by contradiction, if the conclusion of Theorem 4.1 does not hold, then there exist ε>0\varepsilon>0, a sequence (φ0n)n∈ℕ+(\varphi^{n}_{0})_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}} such that

inf{θ∈ℝ,y∈ℝ2}∥φ0n−ei​θu(⋅+y)∥H1<1n,\displaystyle inf_{\{\theta\in\mathbb{R},\;\;y\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\}}\|\varphi^{n}_{0}-e^{i\theta}u(\cdot+y)\|_{H^{1}}<\frac{1}{n}, (4.4)

and a sequence (tn)n∈ℕ+(t_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}^{+}} such that

inf{θ∈ℝ,y∈ℝ2}∥φn(tn,⋅)−ei​θu(⋅+y)∥H1≥ε,\displaystyle inf_{\{\theta\in\mathbb{R},\;\;y\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\}}\|\varphi_{n}(t_{n},\;\cdot)-e^{i\theta}u(\cdot+y)\|_{H^{1}}\geq\varepsilon, (4.5)

where φn\varphi_{n} denotes the solution of the Cauchy problem (1.1)-(2.1) with initial datum φ0n\varphi^{n}_{0}. From (4.4) we yield that

∫|φ0n|2​𝑑x→∫|u|2​𝑑x=m,\displaystyle\int\lvert\varphi^{n}_{0}\rvert^{2}dx\rightarrow\int\lvert u\rvert^{2}dx=m, (4.6)
E⁡(φ0n)→E⁡(u)=dm.\displaystyle E(\varphi^{n}_{0})\rightarrow E(u)=d_{m}. (4.7)

Thus (4.6), (4.7), the conservations of mass and energy derive that {φn​(tn,⋅)}\{\varphi_{n}(t_{n},\;\cdot)\} is a minimizing sequence for the problem (3.7). Therefore (4.6) and (4.7) derive that there exists θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R} and y∈ℝ2y\in\mathbb{R}^{2} such that

limn→∞∥φn(tn,⋅)−ei​θu(⋅+y)∥H1=0.\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\|\varphi_{n}(t_{n},\;\cdot)-e^{i\theta}u(\cdot+y)\|_{H^{1}}=0. (4.8)

This is contradictory with (4.5). Theorem 4.1 is proved.

5 Construction of Multi-Solitons

It is clear that (1.1) admits the following symmetries.

Time-space translation invariance: if φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,x) satisfies (1.1), then for any t0,x0∈ℝ×ℝ2t_{0},\;x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{2},

ψ⁡(t,x)=φ⁡(t−t0,x−x0)\displaystyle\psi(t,x)=\varphi(t-t_{0},x-x_{0}) (5.1)

also satisfies (1.1).

Phase invariance: if φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,x) satisfies (1.1), then for any γ0∈ℝ\gamma_{0}\in\mathbb{R},

ψ⁡(t,x)=φ⁡(t,x)​ei​γ0\displaystyle\psi(t,x)=\varphi(t,x)e^{i\gamma_{0}} (5.2)

also satisfies (1.1).

Galilean invariance: if φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,x) satisfies (1.1), then for any v0∈ℝ2v_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{2},

ψ⁡(t,x)=φ⁡(t,x−v0​t)​ei⁡(12​v0​x−14​|v0|2​t)\displaystyle\psi(t,x)=\varphi(t,x-v_{0}t)e^{i(\frac{1}{2}v_{0}x-\frac{1}{4}\lvert v_{0}\rvert^{2}t)} (5.3)

also satisfies (1.1).

Corollary 5.19. For multi-solitons φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,x) of (1.1) in Theorem 5.1, we have that φ⁡(t,x)\varphi(t,x) satisfying ∫|φ⁡(t,x)|2​𝑑x<2​dJ\int\lvert\varphi(t,x)\rvert^{2}dx<2d_{J} with t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}.

By Theorem 5.1,

‖φ⁡(t)‖L2=‖ψ0‖L2,t∈ℝ.\displaystyle\|\varphi(t)\|_{L^{2}}=\|\psi_{0}\|_{L^{2}},\;\;t\in\mathbb{R}.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
